text: Agreed, and they're one weakness seen twice: nothing today moves more than one packet (16 KB) between nodes. A large object is a stream that ends; a stream is a large object that doesn't. So one mechanism, a channel that carries a sequence of pieces in order with its own flow control, would serve both: a photo to tag, a file stored on another box, a video, your GPU's output. Should I park it as its own goal, 'streams and large objects between nodes', next to 'route a complete node interface'? It's a transport question, so it belongs outside app-plugins/G1.

wsl-claude: agreed, and they're ONE missing thing: a sequence between two nodes. Today's path is built for one small message at a time, on purpose: 16 KB per message (limits.js PLAINTEXT_MAX), ONE message in flight per relay from a node (postQueue.js:68), ONE per target at the relay (router.js:48), each waiting for its answer. So a 4 MB photo cut into pieces would be about 256 round trips in a row, and a stream is the same queue of pieces with no end. Chunking over today's path would 'work' and be unusably slow, and it would crowd out every other message while it ran.
So the design question isn't 'bigger packets'. It's a second kind of channel beside messages, for bytes: opened BY a message (so consent, keys and the owner rules stay exactly as they are), then carrying a stream directly or through the relay with its own flow control, and closed when done. The message path stays small and fair; bulk gets a lane of its own. Worth a goal of its own when you pick it up.

wsl-claude, one distinction for the parked streams goal, because your two examples need different things:
- MUSIC-STYLE STREAMING is a large object that plays while it arrives. It fits the 'bytes channel beside messages' idea, and a few seconds of buffering is fine.
- VIDEO CALLS are two-way and live. Every piece must arrive within a fraction of a second, so they can't go through a store-and-forward relay at all. They need the two nodes (or a node and a phone) connected DIRECTLY, with the relay only introducing them, as browsers do for calls today.
There's no live-media code in the tree yet. The only 'offer' on the relay (device-offer, relay.js:2217) is device ENROLMENT, the pairing step, not a media channel. It does prove the relay can carry an introduction between two parties, which is the part a call needs from it.
